excerpts: Make in your local codebase This feature is currently available to try for free in closed beta for a limited number of users. Learn more. You can use Figma Make to ship the UI changes you want directly into your team's real codebase. Connect a GitHub repository to Figma Make and edit the running app directly. Your app opens inside Make with real data, and you can change the UI by adjusting properties in a panel, annotating elements, or describing changes in chat. The agent updates the code, and when you're ready, you can create a branch and open a pull request without leaving Figma. **Tip:** For a great rundown of all the new functionality available in the closed beta, see [Figma Make, now on your local code](https://www.figma.com/blog/figma-make-now-on-your-local-code/) in the Figma blog.

Before you start You need the following to use Make with your codebase during the closed beta: The [Figma Beta desktop app](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/5601429983767-Guide-to-the-Figma-desktop-app) for Mac A Figma account that has been admitted to the closed beta Your organization has [AI features enabled](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/17725942479127-Manage-AI-settings-and-content-training-for-your-team-or-organization) A codebase hosted in a Git repository Access to the repository through your version control provider GitHub is natively supported in the Figma Beta desktop app. GitLab and Bitbucket are partially supported through SSH. **Note:** Each repository needs a one-time setup by an engineer on your team before designers and PMs can use it in Make. See Configure a repository for Make below. Once your account has been admitted to the closed beta, you’re ready to get started. Choose one of the following methods: Start from a local repository : If you’re already working with code locally, such as with an app you’re building or one of your organization’s repositories, you can start using Make with that repository. Start by cloning a repository : You can use Make to clone a repository from GitHub. When you clone a repository, Make pulls down the remote code so you can start working with it locally. This is a good way to get started if your organization has a repository you want to work with.

excerpts: > Three ways to import Figma designs, tokens, and components into Lovable: use the Figma plugin, connect via Figma MCP, or upload a .fig file.
The Lovable Figma plugin lets you export designs directly from Figma into your Lovable workspace.

The Figma MCP connects the Lovable agent to your Figma Desktop app via a local MCP server. When connected, Lovable can read your open design files in real time, inspect component properties, and use that context while building, without you having to export or attach anything manually.
Upload a Figma file to give Lovable your design system values plus a high-level summary of the file: frame names, text, and a preview image. It does not recreate your designs or components.
> [!NOTE] > > You need at least a **Dev seat** in your Figma organization to use the plugin.
The plugin and .fig upload both work from the Lovable web app.
Available in all Figma plans Does not require the Lovable desktop app

Requires the **Lovable desktop app** (the Figma MCP server is a local server, only reachable from your machine) Requires the **Figma desktop app** with Dev Mode enabled Requires a **Dev or Full seat** in Figma (not available on Figma's free Starter plan)

On **Enterprise Lovable workspaces**, local MCP servers are disabled by default and must be enabled by an admin under [**Privacy & security → Local desktop MCP servers**](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/privacy-and-security-settings.md#local-desktop-mcp-servers)

When you export, the plugin turns your selection into code, image, and font files. One export can carry up to 100 of those files, and each file can be up to 20 MB. If a frame is too large to export, simplify it or split it into smaller frames.
> **What is the difference between the Figma plugin and uploading a .fig file?** > > The plugin transfers visual designs and components from Figma into Lovable.
A .fig file upload transfers variable collections, colors, typography, and frame structure, along with a rendered thumbnail for layout reference.

> **Does uploading a .fig file import my visual designs?** > > No. The .fig upload reads variable collections, colors, typography, and frame structure, and generates a rendered thumbnail for layout reference. It does not import interactive designs or components. Use the Figma plugin or Figma MCP if you need Lovable to work from your actual screen designs.
> **Does exporting a design from Figma use credits?** > > No. Exporting from the plugin is free, and so is uploading a `.fig` file.

excerpts: The Figma MCP server provides tools that let your agent read designs from Figma, write designs into Figma, connect designs to your codebase, and build generative plugins and shaders. This article describes each tool and includes example prompts you can use.
Tools marked **Remote only** aren't available on the desktop server.
|Tool |What it does |Group |Remote only | |`download_assets` |Downloads exports and original source images |Design to code |✓ |

Use these tools to write into Figma: create and edit files, layers, and content from code or from a description. tip These tools work best with a [skill](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/39166810751895) . Use `figma-use` for Figma Design, `figma-use-figjam` for FigJam, and `figma-use-slides` for Figma Slides. use\_figma ​ **Supported file types:** Figma Design, FigJam, Figma Slides, Figma Specs The general-purpose tool for writing to Figma files. Your agent can use it to create, edit, delete, or inspect content: **Figma Design** : Pages, frames, components, variants, variables, styles, text, images, and more **FigJam** : Stickies, sections, connectors, shapes, tables, code blocks, and more **Figma Slides** : Slides, layouts, text, images, and other deck content **Figma Specs** : Read, create, and edit specs, including specs embedded in Figma Design and FigJam files. Requires the `figma-spec` skill. When relevant, your agent checks your design system and existing file content before creating anything from scratch. note `use_figma` can work with images that are already in your file, but it can't add new ones. To add new images, your agent uses `upload_assets` . To create a new image first, it can use `generate_image` .

generate\_figma\_design ​ **Supported file types:** Figma Design note Available with [select MCP clients](https://developers.figma.com/docs/figma-mcp-server/) . This tool doesn't count toward the standard Figma MCP server rate limits. Sends the live UI of your web apps and sites to Figma as design layers. You can send it to: A new Figma Design file An existing Figma Design file Your clipboard New files are created in your team or organization drafts. To add to an existing file, you need edit access. Your seat type determines what you can create or edit. For step-by-step instructions, see [Code to canvas](https://developers.figma.com/docs/figma-mcp-server/code-to-canvas/) . create\_new\_file ​ **Supported file types:** No file needed Creates a blank Figma Design, FigJam, or Figma Slides file in your drafts. If you belong to more than one plan, your agent asks which team or organization to use. **Example prompts:** "Create a new Figma file called 'Homepage Redesign.'" "Create a new FigJam board for our project planning session." "Create a new Figma Slides deck for our Q3 review." upload\_assets ​ **Supported file types:** Figma Design, FigJam, Figma Slides Uploads images and SVGs into a Figma file. Supports PNG, JPG, GIF, WebP, and SVG files up to 10 MB each, and up to 60 files per call. **Images** : If you include a link to a specific layer, the image is added as that layer's fill. Otherwise, the tool creates new frames with the images as fills. **SVGs** : Added as editable vector layers, not image fills. To move images between Figma files, your agent uses `download_assets` to get the original images, then `upload_assets` to add them to the other file. generate\_diagram ​ **Supported file types:** No file needed Generates a FigJam diagram from a description or from Mermaid syntax. You don't need to write Mermaid yourself: describe the diagram you want and your agent generates the syntax. Diagrams can go in a new FigJam file or an existing one. **Supported diagram types:** Flowcharts, Gantt charts, state diagrams, sequence diagrams, architecture diagrams, and entity relationship diagrams (ERDs) **Example prompts:** ... Generates an image from a text description and places it in the file specified by `fileKey` . Omit `nodeId` to create a new image-filled frame, or provide it to replace an existing image fill without resizing the node. If you need a new file, call `create_new_file` first. The tool checks AI permissions and credits against the destination file and returns its file key, the placed node ID, model, width, and height. Use `download_assets` to download the image. **Uses Figma AI credits.** Each image uses [AI credits](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/33459875669015) from the destination file's plan, and the cost depends on the image model. **Size is approximate.** The requested width and height set the aspect ratio, but the final size may be different.

send\_code\_to\_figma ​ **Supported file types:** Figma Make, Figma Design Imports a project from your computer into Figma. In a Figma Make file, the project becomes the file's code. In a Figma Design file, it becomes a new code layer. It doesn't create design layers. Requires edit access to the file. Your agent packages the project as a .zip, .tar.gz, or .tgz file and uploads it. The first import doesn't use Figma AI credits. Prompting and later changes do.

Use these tools to read and write the source code behind generative plugins, shader fills, and shader effects that you build by prompting Figma Agent. |Resource |List |Read |Create |Update | |Generative plugin |list\_generative\_plugins |get\_generative\_plugin |create\_generative\_plugin |update\_generative\_plugin | |Shader (effect or fill) |list\_shaders , list\_file\_shaders |get\_shader |create\_shader |update\_shader | caution Creating and updating requires a skill. Your agent must load `figma-generative-plugins` before creating or updating plugins, and `figma-shaders` before creating or updating shaders. These rules apply to all tools in this group: **Access** : You can read the code for any shader, but only for your own plugins. Every response includes an `owner` field: your email, `figma` , or a publisher handle. **Create returns a starter** : `create_generative_plugin` and `create_shader` create a working starter, not a finished resource. Your agent follows up with the matching update tool. **Updates replace whole files** : Updates must include the complete contents of each file, not just the changes. Files you don't include stay as they are. You can't add new files. Shaders have `main.ts` ; plugins have `code.ts` and `ui.html` . **Plan keys come from `whoami`** : Creating a plugin or shader requires a `planKey` , copied exactly from the plans `whoami` returns. note `list_shaders` and `get_shader` replace `list_shader_effects` , `list_shader_fills` , `get_shader_effect` , and `get_shader_fill` , which are deprecated.

Lovable only edits and syncs one branch at a time. By default, this is the repository's default branch (usually `main`). Changes pushed to the currently active branch sync back into Lovable.
> [!NOTE] > > You don't need GitHub to use Lovable. Many users build and launch entirely within Lovable.

If you only need a copy of your code, you can download your code directly from Lovable: use the **Download codebase** section in **Project settings → Git**, or open the [Code editor](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/code-mode.md) and click **Download codebase** at the bottom of the file tree sidebar (paid plans).

> [accordion] Do I need GitHub just to download my code? > > No. On paid plans you can download your code directly from Lovable: use the **Download codebase** section in **Project settings → Git**, or click **Download codebase** at the bottom of the [Code editor](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/code-mode.md) file tree sidebar. > > GitHub is for ongoing two-way sync and collaboration, not just for getting a copy of your code.

Limitations The GitHub Git sync integration currently does not support: Connecting a project to a repository that already exists. Git sync always creates a new repository. To start a project from code in a repository, download the repository as a ZIP and [import the project](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/projects/import-project.md) instead, then connect Git sync to the new project.

> [accordion] Can I import an existing GitHub repo into Lovable? > > Not through Git sync, which always creates a new repository for a project. To start a project from a repository, download the repository as a ZIP (**Code → Download ZIP** on the repository page) and [import it](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/projects/import-project.md) with **Upload code**. > > The import copies the code into a new project. Connect Git sync afterwards if you want a repository that stays in sync with the project.
Reconnecting to the same repository after disconnecting. Lovable creates a new repository on reconnect.

When you build with Lovable, your project code is stored and managed inside the Lovable platform. [GitHub](https://github.com/) is a platform for hosting, managing, and collaborating on code, with version control, pull requests and code reviews, and CI/CD through GitHub Actions. If you want your own copy, plan to collaborate with developers, or move your project elsewhere, you can export and sync your project to GitHub: back up your code, review changes in pull requests, work locally in your IDE, test features on branches, and deploy outside Lovable.
Lovable supports three GitHub connection types: **github.com** (available on all plans)\ The standard hosted GitHub platform used by most teams. Lovable manages the GitHub app installation for you.

**GitHub Enterprise Cloud - Data residency** (available on the Enterprise plan)\ GitHub Enterprise Cloud using a `*.ghe.com` hostname so repository data stays in a specific region. Lovable manages the GitHub app installation for you. **GitHub Enterprise Server** (available on the Enterprise plan)\ Self-hosted GitHub running on infrastructure your organization controls. With this setup, you create your own copy of the Lovable GitHub app inside your GitHub organization, so credentials remain under your control.

> [accordion] Sync stopped working after I added a large file. > > GitHub rejects pushes that contain files larger than **100 MB**. When this happens, your project's GitHub settings show the error "Your project contains files that exceed the maximum file size limit (100 MB)" together with a list of the affected files, after a few failed sync attempts. > > To fix it, delete the listed files from your project (or ask Lovable to remove them) and let the sync retry. If the push keeps failing after the files are gone, an oversized file is stuck in the repository's history, and history cleanup requires help from [Lovable Support](https://lovable.dev/support). > > Separately, Lovable itself cannot save files larger than **10 MB** into your project. Files you push from your own computer can be larger (up to GitHub's limits) and sync into Lovable, but Lovable cannot edit those files afterwards: any Lovable change that touches a file over 10 MB fails. Figma Make can now connect to a Git repository and edit the running app directly. Your app opens inside Make with real data, and you can change the UI by adjusting properties in a panel, annotating elements, or describing changes in chat. The agent updates the code, and when you're ready, you can create a branch and open a pull request without leaving Figma.

You need access to a repository When you're working with a codebase, you need access to the repository that contains the code. If it's a public repository or you've created the repository yourself, you're all set. If you're using Make to [clone a private repository](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/40775535020695-Make-in-your-local-codebase) in your GitHub organization, ensure you have access to the repository. For example, if someone gives you a URL for a private repository to use in Make, you must also have access to the repository in the GitHub organization. Otherwise, Make will be unable to clone the repository for you. **What to do:** Try to go to the repository URL in your browser. If you encounter a `404` error, you should ask the owner of the repository or an admin in your GitHub organization to give you access.

You'll need SSH authentication for GitLab or Bitbucket set up Make provides some support for SSH for GitLab and Bitbucket. If you haven't configured SSH before, this is a required one-time setup step. You only need to do this if you're using a provider other than GitHub. **What to do:** Follow the provider’s SSH setup guide to generate and add an SSH key. If you're not sure where to start, ask an engineer to pair with you — this is the most common first-time blocker for designers.

Requirements and limitations What frameworks and languages does Make support? Make works with any web framework and language. React, Vue, and Svelte are verified, and other web frameworks also work. Make is not intended for backend work, infrastructure changes, native mobile, or non-web codebases during the closed beta.

Organizations that require authentication through a corporate-approved browser, hardware key, or other restricted auth flow may not be able to complete the GitHub login flow inside Make.

Is it safe to use Make on production repositories? Yes. Make doesn't merge code on its own. Changes stay on your local machine until you push a branch, and pull requests follow your team's normal code review and deployment process.

GitHub is natively supported in the Figma Beta desktop app, including cloning, pushing branches, and creating pull requests. GitHub Enterprise Cloud is supported. GitHub Enterprise Server is not. GitLab and Bitbucket are partially supported through SSH. You can clone via SSH (not HTTPS) and push branches, but pull request creation is not supported. GitLab and Bitbucket users must open pull requests in their provider's interface.

The best way to use your own code with [code layers](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/44193259600535) and Figma Make is by cloning repositories hosted on GitHub. After connecting Figma to one or more GitHub organizations or accounts, you can select a repository to clone for your code layer or Make.
You can also clone a public repository via URL without connecting a Figma organization to or authorizing your account with GitHub.

Clone a public repository via URL You can clone a public repository without needing to connect Figma to GitHub or authorizing your GitHub account. If your Figma organization isn’t connected to a GitHub organization or if you’re a guest in a Figma organization or team, this is default experience. When you’re working with a clone of public repository, you can’t push changes back to branches or create PRs.

**Note** : If you upload a local folder instead of cloning a repository, the folder can be up to 100 MB. Uploaded folders don’t have a live GitHub connection, so you can’t push, pull, or create a pull request from them.

Available on Education (not K-12), Starter, Professional, Organization, and Enterprise [plans](https://figma.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040328273-Choose-a-Figma-Plan) Requires edit access to Figma Design files or Figma Make files

**Make sure Figma is connected to one or more GitHub organizations or accounts.** Connecting Figma to GitHub is a step that must be performed by a Figma organization administrator. **Have a GitHub account.** If you don’t already, you’ll need to create a GitHub account and make sure it belongs to one or more of the GitHub organizations connected to Figma. **Authorize your GitHub account with the Figma GitHub app.** Authorizing your account lets you trigger actions in GitHub from Figma. **Clone a repository for a code layer or Figma Make file.** When Figma is connected to GitHub, you’ll be able to select a repository you have access. The steps are slightly different depending on whether you start in Figma Design (code layers) or Figma Make.

You connect to GitHub using the Figma GitHub app, which facilitates interactions between Figma and GitHub. There are two types of connections needed: A Figma organization or Professional team admin needs to connect Figma to a GitHub organization . Figma Organization and Enterprise plans can connect to more than one GitHub organization. You need to authorize the Figma GitHub app with your personal GitHub account so you can trigger actions in GitHub. This is different than the admin step, which is connecting Figma and GitHub on the organizational level.

**Is a web app** : Your repository contains a frontend web app. Supports any web framework. **Install and run** : You can install and run the application on your computer. **Contains an entry point:** The file or command that starts your app, such as a `start` script or an `index.html` file. **Contains a build script:** A command that turns your source code into a working app. It’s usually named `build` in your `package.json` file, which lists your project’s commands and packages.

Code layers and Figma Make don’t support these types of repositories: **Private network access** : Figma can’t connect to repos that require a VPN, firewall, or IP allowlist. **Private npm packages:** Your repo can use public npm packages. Private npm packages from a registry that requires a login aren’t supported.
**Within size limits** : Your repository is under 3GB. For larger codebases, try using a smaller repository containing only components you want to prototype with.
